name: Hana Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Fenway Growers, field vegetables for two of the big supermarkets. Leeks, carrots, cabbages, a bit of broccoli in summer. Right now it's leek season, so I'm in the field at half six with a crew of six, lifting, trimming and boxing, and then in the packhouse after lunch. You go home with mud up to your elbows and leek smell in your hair.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been there, and what did you do before?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Two and a half years. Before that I was fifteen years in a shoe shop in town, Barker's, until it shut. There was nothing else going round here for a woman my age with no qualifications, so a friend got me in at Fenway. I'm still the slow one on the trimming line. The Polish lads do twice what I do and they're kind about it, which is worse.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's honest work, you can see the full pallet at the end of the day. What wears me out is the cold, and the supermarket rules. A whole lorry of leeks came back last month because they were two centimetres too long. My husband Stefan drives buses, and we live on his wage and mine with nothing over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good for them, it's nothing to do with me. I don't use it, I don't need it. Leeks don't get lifted by a search engine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as what I'd say, really. I've never used one of those AI things and I won't start. If it changes nothing, fine, I've got enough to keep up with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Keep going at Fenway, try to get faster on the line so the supervisor stops watching me. Maybe get my forklift ticket if they pay for it, which is about three hundred pounds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Fed up about other things, but calm about this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What are the other things you're fed up about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The supermarket, mostly. They change the rules on size every season and we eat the cost. And the energy bill, it went up again in October, and Stefan said we'll just wear jumpers indoors, like that's a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you know anyone who uses these tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My Lukas does, for his homework, and I'm not sure that's allowed. The office at Fenway probably does. I asked him once to show me and he went too fast, so I left him to it.

S0.say: I'd say good for them, it's nothing to do with me. I don't use it, and leeks don't get lifted by a search engine.
S0.think: I think the same in private. I've never used AI, I won't start, and I've got enough to keep up with already.
S0.do: Keeps working at Fenway and tries to get faster on the trimming line. Asks if the farm would pay the roughly three hundred pounds for a forklift ticket.
S0.feel: Calm about this, though fed up about other things.
S0.quote: Leeks don't get lifted by a search engine.
S0.fieldNote: Hana speaks in short, blunt sentences and doesn't dress anything up. Her complaints are the supermarket's size rules and energy bills, not technology. She is clearly self-conscious about being the slowest on the line, and that seems to weigh on her more than anything in the card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame for the youngsters, but every generation has something. My dad lost his job at the brickworks and found another one. You get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be all right, because nobody's making a machine for my little job anytime soon if it's all slow. What bothers me is Lukas. He's fourteen and he's not one for books.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep my head down. I wouldn't put myself forward for anything new, I'd just make sure I'm never late and never sick. I'd tell Lukas to get a Saturday job now, at the garden centre or the chippy, so he's got something on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy. Mostly for Lukas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd never put yourself forward. Why not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the last time I did, at Barker's, I asked to do the ordering, and three months later they shut the place. I know it wasn't because of me. But I'd rather be the one nobody notices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Stefan say about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stefan would say don't borrow trouble. He's calmer than me. He'd say the buses will always need a driver, and I'd say that's what I thought about shoe shops.

S1.say: I'd say it's a shame for the young ones, but every generation has something. My dad lost his job at the brickworks and found another, so you get on with it.
S1.think: I think I'd be all right, because a slow change won't reach my little job soon. What bothers me is Lukas, who's fourteen and not one for books.
S1.do: Keeps her head down, never late and never sick, and avoids putting herself forward. Tells her son to get a Saturday job now so he has something on paper.
S1.feel: A little uneasy, mostly for her son.
S1.quote: I know it wasn't because of me. But I'd rather be the one nobody notices.
S1.fieldNote: Her wish to stay unnoticed comes from a specific moment, asking for more responsibility just before the shoe shop closed. She is middle-of-the-road and slow to blame anyone, falling back on 'you get on with it'. The worry is mainly for her son.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say both sides have a point. People need work, but you can't stop progress either. I wouldn't post about it, I'm not on there much, and when I am it's just shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it doesn't touch me, it touches the office at Fenway. The girls who do the orders and the supermarket paperwork could go. I'd miss Carol, she always saves me a biscuit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much. I'd keep working. If Carol lost her job I'd help her look, maybe ask at the packhouse if they need anyone. I wouldn't change anything for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, for other people. I'd feel a bit guilty saying it's fine for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the office is run by a computer, does anything change for you on the line?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the orders change faster. The supermarket already rings at four o'clock wanting another two pallets by morning. If a computer does that, it'll ring at midnight and we'll be the ones lifting in the dark.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame for the layoffs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, honestly. The companies, a bit. The government should have seen it coming. But I can't say I'd turn down cheaper shopping either, so maybe all of us.

S2.say: I'd say both sides have a point: people need work, but you can't stop progress. I wouldn't post about it, because online it's mostly shouting.
S2.think: It touches the office at Fenway, not me, and I'd miss Carol, who saves me a biscuit. My worry is the orders coming faster and later, with us on the line paying for it.
S2.do: Keeps working as usual. Helps Carol look for work if she's laid off, including asking at the packhouse.
S2.feel: Uneasy for others, and a bit guilty that she's fine.
S2.quote: If a computer does that, it'll ring at midnight and we'll be the ones lifting in the dark.
S2.fieldNote: Her middle-ground politics show in spreading blame thinly, including on shoppers like herself. The midnight order line was a sharp insight from someone who rarely thinks about technology. Her plan for herself is to change nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say whoever's in charge needs to sort it out fairly, and quick. People losing jobs and houses going up at the same time is a recipe for trouble. I'd say that at the school gate, that's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd feel safe for once, which is a funny thing to feel lifting leeks. But I'd worry Fenway gets flooded with people who've lost office jobs, younger and quicker than me. I'm already the slowest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Fenway for a proper contract, I'm on a rolling one. I'd do every extra hour going for a year, to get some money in the bank, even a few hundred. And I'd tell Stefan no holiday this year, not even the caravan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Safe and not safe at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's a recipe for trouble. What kind of trouble?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Angry people. You saw it when the factory in Hollin closed, there was graffiti on the job centre and fights in the pub car park. I don't want my kids growing up in that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would it mean, cancelling the caravan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a week in a static caravan by the sea, every August, for twelve years. Mia would cry. But it's four hundred pounds, and four hundred pounds is a month of food.

S3.say: I'd say whoever's in charge should sort it out fairly and quickly. Job losses and rising house prices together are a recipe for trouble.
S3.think: I'd feel safe for once, which is a funny thing to feel lifting leeks. But people who lost office jobs would come to Fenway, younger and quicker than me.
S3.do: Asks Fenway for a proper contract instead of her rolling one. Works every extra hour for a year to save a few hundred, and cancels the family's four hundred pound caravan week.
S3.feel: Anxious. Safe and not safe at the same time.
S3.quote: Four hundred pounds is a month of food.
S3.fieldNote: Her mood went up a step even though physical work is spared, because she sees herself as the weakest on the line. The caravan holiday was the first thing she'd cut, and saying her daughter would cry clearly cost her. She remembers unrest after a local factory closed and fears it coming back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow down, give people time. You can't just switch everyone off. I'd sign a petition if someone brought it round, I wouldn't start one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd be one of the first to go. They already have a camera machine in the packhouse that sorts carrots by size. A robot that trims leeks wouldn't be slower than me, and it wouldn't need a cup of tea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at care homes, but you say robots are going there too. So honestly, I don't know. I'd go to the job centre in the first week and take whatever they have, cleaning, anything. We'd ask Stefan's mum if we could move in with her if the mortgage went.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the shoe shop again, but with nowhere to go this time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd take anything. What would you not do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't go on benefits if I could help it. Not because it's wrong, Stefan's sister needed them, but because I'd feel I'd given up. I'd clean toilets first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them Mum's looking for a new job, like last time. Lukas would know it's worse than that. Mia would ask if we still get the dog, and I wouldn't know what to say.

S4.say: I'd say slow down and give people time, because you can't just switch everyone off. I'd sign a petition if someone brought it round, but I wouldn't start one.
S4.think: I'd be one of the first to go. The packhouse already sorts carrots with a camera, and a robot that trims leeks wouldn't be slower than me.
S4.do: Goes to the job centre in the first week and takes anything, such as cleaning. Plans to ask her mother-in-law about moving in if the mortgage fails.
S4.feel: Alarmed. Like the shoe shop closing again, but with nowhere to go.
S4.quote: A robot that trims leeks wouldn't be slower than me, and it wouldn't need a cup of tea.
S4.fieldNote: This is the big jump, from anxious to alarmed, as expected for packhouse and field work. She had no plan beyond the job centre and her mother-in-law, and admitted it. She'd rather clean toilets than claim benefits, out of pride, not judgement of others.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots one. What would help? Somebody telling us early, a year early, so we could look around before it happens. And a real course near here, not two buses away, that leads to an actual job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: No. Well, maybe that the supermarkets set all the rules and nobody asks them anything. Ask them what they'd do with the robots. I bet they'd want cheaper leeks, not happier workers.

headlineQuote: A robot that trims leeks wouldn't be slower than me, and it wouldn't need a cup of tea.
portrait: Hana Schmidt is 43 and has worked in fields and the packhouse at a supermarket vegetable grower for two and a half years, since the shoe shop she worked in for fifteen years shut. She lives with her husband Stefan, a bus driver, and their two children, with a mortgage and nothing put by. She never uses AI and prefers to stay unnoticed, keeping her head down through the early scenarios. As office jobs go she worries for others and for younger rivals arriving at the farm, and when robots arrive she expects to be first out with no plan beyond the job centre.
biggestWorry: The robots scenario, because she's the slowest on the line and a machine could already do her job.
whatWouldHelp: Being told a year ahead so she could look around, and a local course that leads to a real job.
